module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 313

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/313](https://www.erdosproblems.com/313)
- [A54377](https://oeis.org/A54377) (Primary pseudoperfect numbers)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos313

/--
This set contains all solutions `(m, P)` to the Erdős problem 313.
A solution is a pair where `m` is an integer `≥ 2` and `P` is a non-empty, finite set of
distinct prime numbers, such that the sum of the reciprocals of the primes in `P` equals `1 - 1/m`.
-/
def erdos313Solutions : Set (ℕ × Finset ℕ) :=
  {(m, P) | 2 ≤ m ∧ P.Nonempty ∧ (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) ∧ ∑ p ∈ P, (1 : ℚ) / p = 1 - 1 / m}

/--
Are there infinitely many pairs `(m, P)` where `m ≥ 2` is an integer
and `P` is a set of distinct primes such that the following equation holds:
$\sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} = 1 - \frac{1}{m}$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_313 : answer(sorry) ↔ erdos313Solutions.Infinite := by
  sorry

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_313.variants.solution_6_2_3 : (6, {2, 3}) ∈ erdos313Solutions := by
  norm_num [erdos313Solutions]

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_313.variants.solution_42_2_3_7 : (42, {2, 3, 7}) ∈ erdos313Solutions := by
  norm_num [erdos313Solutions]

/--
An integer `n` is a **primary pseudoperfect number** if it is the denominator `m` in a
solution `(m, P)` to the Erdős 313 problem.
-/
def IsPrimaryPseudoperfect (n : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ P, (n, P) ∈ erdos313Solutions

/--
It is conjectured that the set of primary pseudoperfect numbers is infinite.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_313.variants.primary_pseudoperfect_are_infinite :
    Set.Infinite {n | IsPrimaryPseudoperfect n} := by
  sorry

/--
There are at least 8 primary pseudoperfect numbers. The first eight terms of
[A54377](https://oeis.org/A54377) are exhibited together with their explicit
prime decompositions.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_313.variants.exists_at_least_eight_primary_pseudoperfect :
    8 ≤ (Set.encard {n | IsPrimaryPseudoperfect n}) := by
  let S : Finset ℕ :=
    {2, 6, 42, 1806, 47058, 2214502422, 52495396602,
      8490421583559688410706771261086}
  have hS : (↑S : Set ℕ) ⊆ {n | IsPrimaryPseudoperfect n} := by
    intro x hx
    simp only [S, Finset.coe_insert, Finset.coe_singleton, Set.mem_insert_iff,
      Set.mem_singleton_iff] at hx
    rcases hx with rfl | rfl | rfl | rfl | rfl | rfl | rfl | rfl
    · exact ⟨{2}, by norm_num [erdos313Solutions]⟩
    · exact ⟨{2, 3}, by norm_num [erdos313Solutions]⟩
    · exact ⟨{2, 3, 7}, by norm_num [erdos313Solutions]⟩
    · exact ⟨{2, 3, 7, 43}, by norm_num [erdos313Solutions]⟩
    · exact ⟨{2, 3, 11, 23, 31}, by norm_num [erdos313Solutions]⟩
    · exact ⟨{2, 3, 11, 23, 31, 47059}, by norm_num [erdos313Solutions]⟩
    · exact ⟨{2, 3, 11, 17, 101, 149, 3109}, by norm_num [erdos313Solutions]⟩
    · exact ⟨{2, 3, 11, 23, 31, 47059, 2217342227, 1729101023519}, by
        refine ⟨by decide, by decide, ?_, ?_⟩
        · intro p hp
          fin_cases hp <;> native_decide
        · native_decide⟩
  calc (8 : ℕ∞)
      = ((S.card : ℕ) : ℕ∞) := by decide
    _ = (↑S : Set ℕ).encard := (Set.encard_coe_eq_coe_finsetCard S).symm
    _ ≤ Set.encard {n | IsPrimaryPseudoperfect n} := Set.encard_le_encard hS

end Erdos313

findings.description: The docstring says "The first eight terms of [A54377] are exhibited together with their explicit prime decompositions". The proof actually lists the first seven terms (2, 6, 42, 1806, 47058, 2214502422, 52495396602) and then 8490421583559688410706771261086. That last number is not the 8th term of A054377. The number 5998279018951962402 = 2·3·11·17·101·157·1979·10093·16879 is primary pseudoperfect even under the file's own definition: `IsPrimaryPseudoperfect 5998279018951962402` is proved by `⟨{2,3,11,17,101,157,1979,10093,16879}, by norm_num [erdos313Solutions]⟩` in my scratch file. It is also smaller than 8490421583559688410706771261086. So the eight exhibited numbers are not the eight smallest primary pseudoperfect numbers. The theorem statement `8 ≤ encard {n | IsPrimaryPseudoperfect n}` is still true and proved, so the mathematics is unaffected; only the docstring's description of the witnesses is wrong.

findings.suggested_fix: Replace the 8th witness with `5998279018951962402` and `P = {2, 3, 11, 17, 101, 157, 1979, 10093, 16879}`. `norm_num [erdos313Solutions]` closes that case, so `native_decide` is no longer needed; I checked that the whole proof compiles with axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. Alternatively, reword the docstring to say "the first seven terms of A054377 and the eight-prime-factor example 8490421583559688410706771261086 are exhibited".

reformulations.difference: The file defines a primary pseudoperfect number as an m for which some nonempty finite set P of primes satisfies Σ_{p∈P} 1/p = 1 − 1/m with m ≥ 2. This is the definition erdosproblems.com uses. OEIS and Wikipedia instead use n > 1 with 1/n + Σ_{p | n} 1/p = 1, a sum over the prime factors of n. In the Lean definition P is not required to be the set of prime divisors of n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Write Q = ∏_{p∈P} p and A = Σ_{q∈P} ∏_{r∈P∖{q}} r. The equation becomes A·m = Q·(m−1). Since gcd(m, m−1) = 1, m divides Q. For each p ∈ P, A ≡ Q/p ≢ 0 (mod p), so p divides m, and therefore Q divides m. Hence m = Q and P = primeFactors m. That gives the OEIS equation. Conversely, P = primeFactors n is a witness. I proved `IsPrimaryPseudoperfect n ↔ 1 < n ∧ 1/n + ∑ p ∈ n.primeFactors, 1/p = 1` in Lean, with only standard axioms.

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether there are infinitely many solutions (m, p_1<…<p_k). This variant instead asserts, as the conjectured positive answer, that the set of m values (primary pseudoperfect numbers) is infinite. The main theorem counts pairs (m, P); the variant counts only m.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every solution has m = ∏P (proved in Lean), and P is the set of prime factors of m. So the projection (m, P) ↦ m is injective on `erdos313Solutions`, and its image is `{n | IsPrimaryPseudoperfect n}`. Therefore `erdos313Solutions.Infinite ↔ {n | IsPrimaryPseudoperfect n}.Infinite`; I proved this in Lean via `Set.infinite_image_iff`. The source makes the same point: "there is at most one solution for each m". The variant is thus exactly the "yes" answer to `erdos_313`.

review.notes: `erdos313Solutions` and `erdos_313` state the erdosproblems.com question exactly. A pair (m, P) with P a nonempty Finset of primes is the same as a solution (m, p_1<…<p_k). `P.Nonempty` follows from `2 ≤ m`: the empty sum is 0, and 0 = 1 − 1/m forces m = 1. Both divisions are in ℚ with nonzero denominators (primes, and m ≥ 2), so no junk values arise. The two test memberships pass, which confirms the ℚ reading. `answer(sorry) ↔ Set.Infinite …` has the right polarity for "Are there infinitely many…?". k is left free, as it must be: for a fixed k there are only finitely many solutions. Status: erdosproblems.com shows OPEN (history unchanged since 2025-10-20), the teorth data says open, and Wikipedia and OEIS say infinitude is unknown. In 2026 two further primary pseudoperfect numbers were found (arXiv:2605.21518, Martins/Wang), but no proof of infinitude, so `research open` is current. The erdosproblems page's remark "there are 8 known" is itself now outdated (10 are known); that is a problem with the source, not the file. The only defect I found is the stale \"first eight terms\" docstring above; my suggested replacement proof also removes the `native_decide` dependency. My scratch proofs are in /workspace/review/: equiv.lean (m = ∏P, the infinitude equivalence, and the OEIS-definition equivalence), scratch4.lean (the new term is primary pseudoperfect) and fix8.lean (the fixed proof).
